```text
1021
1022

1025

Limitations
Our evaluation covers four NER datasets; an exploratory RE extension on SciERC is reported in
Appendix L but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated. We cover 4B–8B scale;
whether the gap holds for 70B+ models or closedsource APIs is untested. Larger models may produce more diverse samples. We do not train a verifier, leaving unknown how much oracle headroom
a supervised approach could recover.
We evaluate at N =8 (primary) and N =16; behavior at larger sample sizes is unknown (Appendix R). The free-form ablation covers SciERC
NER and CoNLL NER with one model; RE freeform results are in Appendix L. Qwen3-8B’s SciERC checkpoint used empty &lt;think>&lt;/think>
blocks; a three-part analysis rules out this confound (Appendix I). LP compression worsens on
easy datasets at lower temperature (CoNLL tied
fractions reach 95.8% at T =0.7); whether reduced temperature translates to selection gains remains untested. We tested verbalized confidence
(Tian et al., 2023) as a second per-sample signal;
it exhibits severe overconfidence (mean 8.58/10
on SciERC, 9.24/10 on CoNLL) and yields the
weakest QE and selection among all signals (Appendix U). Ad-hoc LP×VC combinations yield at
most +0.2 pp over greedy (not significant; §5);
whether learned combinations could close the gap
remains open. The ε=0.05 threshold used for
tied/non-tied LP stratification is a post-hoc exploratory choice; while selection F1 is stable across
ε ∈ [0, 0.2] (Appendix J), the specific subset gains
should be interpreted as characterizing the compression phenomenon rather than as a tuned selection
strategy. We tested one remedy for LP compression
(entity-token-only LP, excluding format/schema tokens) which fails to improve selection despite increasing within-instance variance on SciERC (4×);
LP×VC combinations also fail to recover selection
(§5); calibration-based approaches remain unexplored. Our selection experiments use 2 training
seeds (stability σ≤0.026); while within-seed statistical power is high (n=32,565 for Few-NERD),
training seed stochasticity is not exhaustively quantified. Few-NERD models are trained for 3 epochs
(vs. 5 for other datasets) due to earlier convergence;
a 5-epoch control experiment is provided in Appendix Z to verify that degeneracy differences are
not training-induced.
13

Ethics Statement

1026

All experiments use publicly available benchmarks
(SciERC, CoNLL-2003, WNUT-17) and openweight models (Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B, LLaMA3.1-8B). CoNLL-2003 is derived from the Reuters
RCV1 corpus, which is available for research purposes under a NIST agreement; we use the standard
research distribution. No new human data was collected or annotated for this study. Our findings on
signal limitations could inform more reliable deployment of IE systems by guiding practitioners
toward appropriate confidence signals for their use
case. Code and data will be released upon acceptance at [anonymized URL].

1027

1039

References

1040

Taylor Berg-Kirkpatrick, David Burkett, and Dan Klein.
2012. An empirical investigation of statistical significance in NLP. In Proceedings of the 2012 Joint
Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing and Computational Natural Language Learning (EMNLP-CoNLL), pages 995–1005.
```

```text
1	\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
2	
3	We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation and sample selection in LLM-based NER across four benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient.
4	All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38 on the primary test bed, 0.42 on Few-NERD; AUROC up to 0.82), supporting selective prediction and error flagging.
5	However, quality estimation does not translate to sample selection, and the gap has a three-layer structure: four instance-level signals cannot rank candidates by construction; MBR selection with well-aligned utility ($\rho{=}0.52$) fails because instance degeneracy (14\textendash 47\%) collapses the candidate pool; and LP, the sole per-sample signal, requires two jointly necessary conditions: low degeneracy and adequate LP-quality alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$).
6	LP selection succeeds when both conditions are met: at 13.8\% degeneracy with strong alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.5$; Few-NERD), LP achieves $+1.36$~pp ($p{<}0.001$); at 17.8\% with weak alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.24$; SciERC), $+0.42$~pp ($p{=}0.091$); at 47.4\% (CoNLL), LP fails.
7	In the low-degeneracy regime, LP selection scales with sample budget ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16, paired $p{=}0.003$).
8	Structural signals fail uniformly regardless of degeneracy, and supervised combination of all five signals cannot close the oracle gap; the bottleneck lies in the signal space accessible to unsupervised aggregation, not in the combination method.
9	Whether these patterns persist at 70B+ scales remains open.
10	Closing the gap for structural signals requires content-aware verifiers that examine output semantics \cite{cobbe2021verifiers}; LP provides a lightweight baseline when both degeneracy and alignment conditions are met.
11	
```

```text
1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}

4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Datasets.}
8	We evaluate on four English NER benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient, each serving a distinct role.
9	\textbf{SciERC} \cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test instances, 6 entity types) is the primary medium-difficulty test bed where models achieve ${\approx}$65\% F1.
10	\textbf{Few-NERD} \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (INTRA coarse; 37{,}648 instances, 8 entity types, ${\approx}$75\% F1) provides a low-degeneracy contrast where LP selection succeeds (\S\ref{sec:fewnerd}).
11	\textbf{CoNLL-2003} \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (3{,}453 test sentences, 4 entity types, ${\approx}$91\% F1) serves as a ceiling-effect control where limited oracle headroom constrains selection gains.
12	\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (1{,}287 social media instances, 52\% zero F1) probes the signal-collapse boundary where model capability is insufficient.
13	
14	\paragraph{Models and sampling.}
15	Both \textbf{Qwen3-8B} and \textbf{LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct} are fine-tuned with LoRA (rank$=$32, $\alpha{=}64$) for 5 epochs using LLaMA Factory \cite{zheng2024llamafactory} under identical training procedures.
16	Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint has a minor train--test mismatch (empty thinking tokens); a quantitative analysis rules out this confound (Appendix~\ref{app:thinking_token}).
17	We draw $N{=}8$ samples at $T{=}1.0$ (primary), with $N{=}16$ for scaling experiments.\footnote{$N{=}16$ with 3 seeds verifies scaling and ranking stability ($\sigma{\leq}0.026$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}); gains beyond $N{=}8$ are sublinear (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).}
18	Inference uses vLLM with constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}.\footnote{Quality estimation uses a single primary seed (seed${=}42$); selection uses 2-seed averages for variance estimation. Three-seed experiments ($\sigma{\leq}0.026$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}) confirm ranking stability; the reduced seed count for primary results reflects computational budget.}

53	\subsection{The Correlation-Selection Gap}
54	\label{sec:selection_gap}
55	
56	The gap has three layers: (1)~four instance-level signals cannot rank candidates by construction; (2)~MBR selection fails because degeneracy collapses the candidate pool; (3)~LP requires both low degeneracy and adequate alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$).

84	Despite moderate quality estimation, no signal consistently improves selection over greedy (Table~\ref{tab:selection}, Figure~\ref{fig:selection_gap}).
85	Instance-level signals assign identical QE scores to all candidates; MBR conversion does not improve over greedy on the primary test bed.
86	
87	\paragraph{No significant improvement over greedy.}
88	On SciERC ($n{=}529$, 2-seed sign tests\footnote{Seed variation $\sigma{\leq}0.026$ (Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}); post-hoc power: ${\sim}$55\% at $n{=}529$ for 1~pp effect. Few-NERD ($n{=}32{,}565$) provides ${>}99$\% power and serves as the definitive test.}), the oracle (0.778) reveals 13.3~pp of headroom, yet LP achieves only $+0.2$~pp ($p{=}0.29$).
89	The pattern holds across CoNLL and WNUT-17 (Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}); under stringent TOST anchors, some configurations show significant \textit{degradation} (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).
90	Few-NERD provides the definitive contrast: LP achieves $+1.36$~pp ($p{<}0.001$) at low degeneracy (\S\ref{sec:fewnerd}), while structural signals still fail.
91	Instance-level signals predict \textit{which inputs} the model handles reliably, not \textit{which output} is best; closing this gap likely requires trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers}.\footnote{The sole positive finding (non-tied LP subset, $+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.004$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}) survives Bonferroni correction over 5 comparisons.}

113	\footnotetext{Instance degeneracy: fraction of gold-filtered instances where all $N$ samples produce identical instance-level F1.}
114	
115	Few-NERD (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}) confirms that LP selection effectiveness is inversely associated with degeneracy.
116	Under standard early stopping, Few-NERD degeneracy is 13.8\% (training convergence modulates this rate, Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}), and LP achieves $+1.36$~pp (95\% CI $[+1.18, +1.53]$, $p{<}0.001$), while all structural signals degrade selection (VC $-1.79$, SJ $-2.14$~pp).
117	
118	\paragraph{Two necessary conditions for LP selection.}
119	The cross-dataset gradient is monotonic (47.4\% $\to$ fail, 17.8\% $\to$ $+0.42$~pp, 13.8\% $\to$ $+1.36$~pp; Figure~\ref{fig:degeneracy_scatter}), but low degeneracy alone is not sufficient: the LoRA-rank ablation (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}) reduces degeneracy to 7.2\% yet LP still fails because $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}){\approx}0.24$.
120	Few-NERD satisfies both conditions: low degeneracy (13.8\%) and strong alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.5$); per-type analysis confirms the pattern ($\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$, $n{=}8$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
121	All five signals achieve positive QE on Few-NERD (LP $\rho{=}0.42$, VC $0.39$), yet only LP translates QE into selection; the gap confirms that strong instance-level QE cannot rank candidates within an instance.
122

131	
132	\paragraph{LP selection scales with sample budget.}
133	Doubling $N$ from 8 to 16 on Few-NERD yields $+0.52$~pp (paired $p{=}0.003$, CI $[+0.17, +0.87]$), driven by reduced degeneracy (14.6\% $\to$ 7.0\%) expanding headroom (12.1 $\to$ 15.4~pp), while LP ranking quality remains stable ($\rho{\approx}0.62$).
134	Structural signals remain uniformly negative at $N{=}16$; the gap persists regardless of sample budget.

137	\subsection{Robustness}
138	\label{sec:robustness_main}
139	
140	Consistency signals are robust across $T{\in}\{0.7, 1.0\}$ with sublinear $N$-scaling gains (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}); LP shows the largest temperature sensitivity ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.044$).
141	Signal rankings are stable across seeds (Kendall's $W{=}1.0$ at $N{=}8$, though statistical precision is limited with $m{=}3$ raters, exact $p{\approx}0.028$; Table~\ref{tab:ranking-stability}).
142	NER calibration is reasonable (ECE 0.069--0.096; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}).

148	\label{tab:scale_ablation}

151	& & \textbf{8B} & \textbf{4B} & $\Delta$ \\
152	\midrule
153	CoNLL & SJ & .436 & .422 & $-$.014 \\

156	       & FK & .267 & .326 & $+$.059 \\

160	
161	\paragraph{Scale robustness.}
162	With Qwen3-4B (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}), QE is comparable (mean $|\Delta\rho|{=}0.042$), yet selection remains below greedy despite 13.0~pp headroom. Task difficulty is a stronger predictor than model scale within the 3B--8B range (Appendix~\ref{app:llama3b}).
163	Degeneracy scales with capability: 8B shows 17.8\% vs.\ 4B's 10.4\% on SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
164	
165	\paragraph{LoRA-rank ablation.}
166	Training with LoRA rank${=}8$ (vs.\ 32) lowers degeneracy from 17.8\% to 7.2\% and increases headroom to 16.0~pp, but selection still fails (LP 0.635 vs.\ greedy 0.640).
167	The ablation isolates the second condition: within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}){\approx}0.24$ remains too weak despite wider LP spread (0.057 vs.\ 0.041 nats). Both low degeneracy and adequate alignment are independently necessary.
168	
169	\paragraph{Supervised verifier baseline.}
170	Supervised verifiers (logistic regression, MLP, random forest) trained on all five signals (3-fold CV, SciERC, $N{=}16$, $+17.9$~pp headroom) all perform at or below greedy\footnote{Greedy F1 is 0.644 (3-seed mean), consistent with Table~\ref{tab:selection}.} (LR: $-0.3$~pp; MLP: $-0.6$~pp; RF: $-2.9$~pp).
171	Adding pairwise interaction features does not help (AUROC 0.632 vs.\ 0.639).
172	The bottleneck is in what the signals encode, not how they are aggregated.
```

```text
1	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Implications for practitioners.}
4	All signals achieve positive quality estimation across non-collapsed datasets (LP $\rho{=}0.42$ on Few-NERD, VC $\rho{=}0.38$ on SciERC, EM AUROC${=}0.82$ on CoNLL), with rankings stable across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}).
5	For selection, LP achieves significant gains only when both conditions are met ($+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD, $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); structural signals uniformly degrade selection.
6	RE signal rankings are in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
7	
8	\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
9	Two mechanisms block selection: \textit{instance degeneracy} (consensus-proximity) and \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (per-sample).
10	Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$) and closes 23--41\% of the oracle gap, but 17.8\% (SciERC) to 47.4\% (CoNLL) of instances produce identical F1 across all samples, eliminating headroom entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
11	Degeneracy is determined by the interplay of task structure, model architecture, and training convergence (Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}); cross-model evidence (LLaMA 89.2\% vs.\ Qwen 47.4\% on CoNLL; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}) reinforces the pattern.
12	LP is severely compressed (median range 0.041 nats; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with pooled within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}){=}0.248$.
13	
14	\paragraph{Non-tied subset and $N$-scaling.}
15	Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), within-instance $\rho$ rises to 0.39 and LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$, survives Bonferroni; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}).
16	LP scales with $N$ in the low-degeneracy regime ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16 on Few-NERD, $p{=}0.003$; \S\ref{sec:fewnerd}); on SciERC, even $N{=}32$ captures less than 5\% of headroom (Table~\ref{tab:n_scaling_selection}).
17	An oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp, confirming per-sample signal exists but current signals cannot extract it (full analyses in Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, \ref{app:vc_quartile}).
18	
19	\paragraph{LP compression mechanisms.}
20	Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute: token-level averaging, schema-dominated tokens, vocabulary restriction under constrained decoding, and format-token dilution.
21	Free-form decoding rules out constraint-imposed mechanisms for NER (std ratio 0.97; Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}) but restores LP selection for RE ($+2.35$~pp, $p{=}0.025$; Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
22	Entity-token LP exhibits $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse ($-2.0$~pp SciERC, $-3.3$~pp CoNLL): fine-tuned models assign near-deterministic probabilities at the representation level, and compression cannot be broken by disaggregating to entity tokens.
23	LP failures show cross-seed stability (Jaccard${=}0.42$; Appendix~\ref{app:lp_failure_stability}), consistent with a systematic failure mode.
24	
25	\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
26	At the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17), QE signals collapse (VC conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}); at the ceiling boundary (CoNLL, degeneracy 47--89\%), LP fails entirely.
27	In the moderate regime, two conditions jointly determine effectiveness: the cross-dataset gradient (47\% $\to$ fail, 18\% $\to$ weak, 14\% $\to$ strong) is confirmed at entity-type level ($\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
28	Two independent manipulations (LoRA rank 8: degeneracy 7.2\%, $\rho{=}0.24$; $T{=}1.2$: degeneracy 12.5\%, $\rho{=}0.225$; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}) confirm alignment is largely task-determined; degeneracy reduction alone cannot unlock LP selection on datasets with weak alignment.
29	
30	\paragraph{Practical guidelines.}
31	Practitioners should first estimate instance degeneracy on a labeled subset (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}): in the high-degeneracy regime (${>}$30\%), prefer greedy decoding; structural signals still support quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.43$--$0.47$).
32	In the low-degeneracy regime (${<}$15\%) with adequate alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$), LP selection is effective and scales with $N$ ($+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD; $+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16).
33	Temperature provides a controllable lever for degeneracy (40.3\% at $T{=}0.5$ to 12.5\% at $T{=}1.2$; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}) but cannot address alignment; training convergence offers a second lever (Few-NERD degeneracy rises from 11\% to 31\% between 3 and 5 epochs, halving LP gains; Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound}).
34	Standard calibration methods preserve within-instance argmax and cannot change selection; even multi-feature variants yield no improvement ($p{=}0.31$--$0.83$; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}), confirming the bottleneck is alignment rather than miscalibration.
35	
36	\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
37	The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; even supervised combination of all five signals fails to close the oracle gap (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
38	Effective selection requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N{=}8$ captures most QE benefit (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
39	Structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
40
```

```text
1	\begin{abstract}
2	Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
3	We evaluate five confidence signals (four instance-level, one per-sample log-probability [LP]) for quality estimation and sample selection on four NER benchmarks using 4B\textendash 8B models.
4	All signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38), supporting selective prediction.
5	Quality estimation does not translate to selection, however: despite ${\sim}$13~pp oracle headroom, no signal consistently outperforms greedy decoding.
6	The gap has a three-layer structure: four instance-level signals cannot rank candidates by construction; MBR selection fails because instance degeneracy (14\textendash 47\% identical outputs) eliminates headroom; and LP requires two jointly necessary conditions: low instance degeneracy, and adequate LP-quality alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$).
7	When both conditions are met, LP achieves significant gains ($+1.36$~pp at 14\% degeneracy, $p{<}0.001$); when either is violated, selection fails.
8	Degeneracy is the dominant bottleneck, controllable via temperature and training budget; in the low-degeneracy regime, LP scales with sample count ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16, paired $p{=}0.003$).
9	Closing the gap for structural signals likely requires learned per-sample scoring.
10	\end{abstract}
```

```text
1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
4	But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.
5	
6	Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
7	Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
8	Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we investigate \textit{why} this correlation fails to yield selection improvements, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
9	Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, and separate quality estimation from best-of-$N$ selection.
10	
11	A methodological premise structures our analysis: four of five signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) are instance-level aggregates that by design assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
12	These signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38 on the primary test bed, 0.42 on Few-NERD; AUROC up to 0.82; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction and error flagging.
13	Yet quality estimation does not translate to structural selection, a disparity we term the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (the disparity between a signal's ability to rank instances reliably and its failure to select the best output within a single instance): structural best-of-$N$ selection matches or degrades greedy decoding ($T{=}0$) despite 12\textendash 14~pp oracle headroom.
14	The gap has two empirical causes: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy}, where fine-tuned models produce identical outputs for 14\textendash 47\% of instances, which eliminates selection headroom despite positive within-instance utility\textendash F1 correlation (median $\rho{=}0.52$); and (b)~\textit{weak LP-quality alignment}, where within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ is too low to exploit the remaining headroom (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
15	LP selection requires both low degeneracy and adequate alignment: significant at 13.8\% degeneracy with $\rho{\approx}0.5$ ($+1.36$~pp, $p{<}0.001$), sub-significant at 17.8\% with $\rho{\approx}0.24$ ($+0.42$~pp), and absent at 47.4\%.
16	
17	\begin{figure*}[t]
18	\centering
19	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
20	\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals reliably predict instance-level quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL, 0.38 on the primary test bed, 0.42 on Few-NERD; AUROC up to 0.82). \textbf{Right}: quality estimation does not translate to selection; all methods approximately match greedy decoding ($T{=}0$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).}
21	\label{fig:overview}
22	\end{figure*}
23	
24	We evaluate five signals from three families (structural, surface, and model-internal) on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc} as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (signal-collapse boundary), using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B).
25	We vary candidate pool size ($N{\in}\{2,\ldots,32\}$), signal sophistication, and model capacity within the 4B\textendash 8B range; behavior at 70B+ scales remains an open question.
26	An exploratory extension to relation extraction is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
27	Our contributions:
28	\begin{enumerate}
29	    \item \textbf{Quality estimation framework.}
30	    Five signals from three families evaluated on four NER benchmarks, two model families, and a 4B ablation. Structural signals reliably predict quality (VC $\rho{=}0.38$; EM AUROC${=}0.82$), with model-stable rankings supporting selective prediction.
31	
32	    \item \textbf{Diagnosis of the correlation-selection gap.}
33	    A three-layer failure: instance-level signals cannot rank candidates by construction; MBR fails because degeneracy (14\textendash 47\%) collapses the candidate pool; LP requires both low degeneracy and adequate alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$).
34	    Diagnostic ablations (LoRA rank, free-form decoding, entity-token LP, supervised combination) confirm the bottleneck lies in the signal space, not combination methods.
35	
36	    \item \textbf{Two necessary conditions for LP selection.}
37	    The cross-dataset gradient (47\% $\to$ fail, 14\% $\to$ $+1.36$~pp at $p{<}0.001$) establishes degeneracy as one condition; LoRA-rank and temperature manipulations independently confirm alignment as the other. Entity-type-level analysis provides statistical grounding ($\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$); LP scales with $N$ in the low-degeneracy regime ($+0.52$~pp, $p{=}0.003$).
38	\end{enumerate}
39	
40
```

```text
1	\section{Method}\label{sec:method}
2	
3	\subsection{Problem Formulation}\label{sec:formulation}
4	
5	Given model $\mathcal{M}$ and input $x$, we sample $N$ outputs $\{y_1, \ldots, y_N\}$ at temperature $T > 0$ via constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}, where each $y_i$ is an entity set.
6	A \textbf{per-sample signal} $c_{\text{ps}}: (x, y_i) \to \mathbb{R}$ scores each output independently; an \textbf{instance-level signal} $c_{\text{il}}: (x, \{y_i\}_{i=1}^N) \to \mathbb{R}$ produces a single score per input (notation in Appendix~\ref{app:notation}).
7	This distinction is consequential for selection: in our study, 4 of 5 signals are instance-level aggregates that assign identical QE scores to all $N$ candidates. Consensus-proximity (MBR) converts these to per-sample rankings (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}), but these rankings do not improve selection; only natively per-sample signals can, in principle, exploit oracle headroom.
8	
9	\subsection{Confidence Signals}\label{sec:signals}
10	
11	Four are \textit{consistency signals}: \textit{structural} (Soft Jaccard [SJ], entity voting confidence [VC]) and \textit{surface} (exact match [EM], Fleiss' $\kappa$ [FK]); log-probability [LP] is the sole \textit{model-internal}, per-sample signal.
12	
13	\paragraph{Log-probability (model-internal, per-sample).}
14	For sample $y_i$ with tokens $t_1, \ldots, t_{|y_i|}$:
15	\begin{equation}\label{eq:logprob}
16	c_{\text{lp}}(y_i) = \frac{1}{|y_i|} \sum_{j=1}^{|y_i|} \log p_{\mathcal{M}}(t_j \mid t_{&lt;j}, x)
17	\end{equation}
18	
19	\paragraph{Exact match voting (surface, instance-level).}
20	The proportion of samples producing the most common output:
21	\begin{equation}\label{eq:em}
22	c_{\text{em}}(x) = \frac{1}{N} \max_{y} \big|\{i : y_i = y\}\big|
23	\end{equation}
24	
25	\paragraph{Fleiss' $\kappa$ (surface, instance-level).}
26	We adapt \citet{fleiss1971agreement} to entity sets: items are unique (text, type) tuples across all $N$ samples; each sample assigns binary present/absent labels, yielding a $|E_\cup| \times 2$ rating matrix:
27	\begin{equation}\label{eq:fk}
28	\kappa = \frac{\bar{P} - \bar{P}_e}{1 - \bar{P}_e}
29	\end{equation}
30	where $\bar{P}$ is mean observed and $\bar{P}_e$ expected agreement.
31	Temperature-based sampling introduces mild negative dependence ($-$0.4\% to $-$4.0\%; Appendix~\ref{app:fk_independence}), which does not inflate FK.
32	Unlike structural signals, FK relies on exact string matching.
33	
34	\paragraph{Soft Jaccard (structural, instance-level).}
35	For samples $y_i, y_j$, we group extractions by type, compute max-weight bipartite matching (Hungarian algorithm, token-level IoU), and define:
36	\begin{equation}\label{eq:sj}
37	\text{SJ}(y_i, y_j) = \frac{\sum_{m \in M} \text{sim}(a_m, b_m)}{\sum_{g} \max(|g_i|, |g_j|)}
38	\end{equation}
39	where $M$ is the matched set, $\text{sim}(a_m, b_m)$ is the token-level IoU, and $\max(|g_i|, |g_j|)$ penalizes length asymmetry.\footnote{The two normalizer variants produce nearly identical rankings ($|\Delta\rho|{\leq}0.009$; Table~\ref{tab:sj_normalizer}).}
40	The instance-level QE signal averages over all pairs: $c_{\text{sj}}(x) = \binom{N}{2}^{-1} \sum_{i&lt;j} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
41	For selection, consensus-proximity converts this to per-sample utility $u_{\text{sj}}(y_i) = (N{-}1)^{-1} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$, equivalent to MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling}. The same construction applies to FK, EM, and VC.
42	
43	\paragraph{Entity voting confidence (structural, instance-level).}
44	For each entity $e$ in the union $E_\cup$ of all samples, we compute frequency $\text{freq}(e) = |\{i : e \in y_i\}| / N$.
45	The instance-level confidence is the mean frequency:
46	\begin{equation}\label{eq:voting}
47	c_{\text{vote}}(x) = \frac{1}{|E_\cup|} \sum_{e \in E_\cup} \text{freq}(e)
48	\end{equation}
49	When $E_\cup = \emptyset$, $c_{\mathrm{vc}}(x) = 0$.\footnote{For voted-output \textit{selection}, we include only entities with frequency ${>}N/2$ (standard majority voting).}
50	
51	\subsection{Evaluation Framework}\label{sec:evaluation}
52	
53	\paragraph{Quality estimation.}
54	Spearman $\rho$ between the signal and instance-level F1, and AUROC classifying instances as above/below median F1.
55	Both quality estimation and selection exclude instances with no gold annotations: $n{=}529$ on SciERC (from 551), $n{=}2{,}756$ on CoNLL (from 3{,}453).\footnote{On CoNLL, full-set ($n{=}3{,}453$) Spearman $\rho$ values are higher than gold-filtered ($n{=}2{,}756$) by $+0.03$--$0.05$ due to the zero/non-zero boundary inflating correlations, paralleling the effect documented for WNUT-17 in Appendix~\ref{app:additional}.}
56	
57	\paragraph{Sample selection.}
58	Best-of-$N$ F1: per-sample signals (LP) directly rank candidates; instance-level signals rank via consensus-proximity (MBR utility; see SJ definition above).
59	Baselines: \textit{oracle} (highest-F1 sample) and \textit{greedy} ($T{=}0$ argmax decoding).
60	
```

```text
3	\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}
4	Self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} improves reasoning via majority voting; extensions handle free-form text \cite{chen2024usc, thirukovalluru2024atomic, manakul2023selfcheckgpt}.
5	Test-time scaling studies \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys} and reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty, kim2026reasc, wang2025rankedvoting, oh2026latentsc} all rely on answer-level agreement; \citet{feng2025optimal} and \citet{wang2025make} adapt to difficulty-aware settings; \citet{li2025llms} propose generative self-aggregation for IE but focus on fusion rather than selection.
6	We extend self-consistency to set-valued structured outputs and identify the correlation-selection gap.
7	
8	\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
9	\citet{yao2026consistency} show consistency correlates with accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE; we show correlation is necessary but not sufficient, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as blocking mechanisms.
10	Our experiments use fine-tuned models, where degeneracy is most pronounced and is modulated by task structure and training convergence (Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}).
11	CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses confidence with consistency for QA/summarization; our supervised verifier baseline (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}) suggests combination strategy is not the bottleneck.
12	Earlier work on confidence for structured prediction \cite{culotta2004confidence, mejer2010confidence, fomicheva2020unsupervised} establishes the paradigm we extend to set-valued outputs.
13	Our evaluation builds on generative IE \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided, park2024grammar, schall2025hidden, yun2025price}.
14	
15	\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and MBR decoding.}
16	Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey}, and calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic}; semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic} and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} provide model-internal alternatives.
17	Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}; unlike MT where MBR yields consistent gains \cite{freitag2022high}, instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom MBR needs even when utility is well-aligned ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
18	\citet{eikema2025structured} find MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs; our diagnosis is complementary: degeneracy, not utility misalignment, is the primary bottleneck.
19	Our QE results connect to selective prediction \cite{kuleshov2015calibrated}: signals with AUROC up to 0.82 support abstention policies independent of sample selection.
20	
21	\paragraph{Best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers.}
22	\citet{gao2023scaling} establish BoN scaling laws; our unsupervised signals face a more fundamental limitation than reward overoptimization.
23	Trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify, fernandes2022quality} learn per-sample scoring; our LoRA-rank ablation (degeneracy 7.2\%, selection still fails at $\rho{\approx}0.24$) confirms verifier training is necessary beyond increasing output diversity.
24	Fine-tuning contributes to degeneracy, analogous to diversity collapse in RLHF \cite{kirk2024understanding}; constrained structured outputs limit the diversity that temperature scaling \cite{holtzman2020curious} can recover.
25	
```
